chicken-breast-fried-coated-skin-coating.title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin/coating edible

content.title: About
content.content: Fried chicken breast coated in a crispy breading is a staple of fast‑food and restaurant menus. The breast pieces are dipped in a seasoned flour‑egg mixture, sometimes rolled in breadcrumbs, and then deep‑fried until golden. The edible coating adds flavor, crunch, and extra calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Breaded fried chicken breast is one of the most popular fast‑food items worldwide.
Traditional breading often includes paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, and breadcrumbs for extra taste.
Some establishments double‑fry: a quick deep‑fry followed by a short oven finish for a lighter crust.
Chicken is a lean meat, but frying in oil dramatically increases its caloric density.
Breading can be made gluten‑free using corn starch or rice flour.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: phosphorus and selenium
items.content: Phosphorus is important for bones and teeth, while selenium acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and fat in the coating helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Calories from the oil and carbs in the breading quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying and breading make the dish energy‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Saturated fats and trans fats
items.content: Reused or overheated oil can generate trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Breading often contains salt and flavor enhancers, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Standard wheat‑based breading can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; internal temperature should reach 75 °C (165 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breaded fried chicken breast is usually served hot as a main dish, in burgers, salads, or with dipping sauces such as barbecue, mayo, or mustard. It pairs well with fries, vegetable sides, or rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer bags at –18 °C; reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to retain crispness.

chicken-or-turkey-salad-made-with-light-.title: Chicken or Turkey Salad with Light Mayonnaise Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey salad made with a light mayonnaise‑type dressing is a ready‑to‑eat dish that includes cooked poultry, fresh vegetables (usually lettuce, tomato, cucumber) and a low‑fat creamy sauce. It is packaged for convenience and can be eaten straight from the container.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey provide lean, high‑quality protein that is easy to digest.
Light mayonnaise dressing typically contains fewer calories and less fat than regular mayonnaise.
Salads are often vacuum‑packed, extending shelf life without the need for added preservatives.
Seasonings such as dill, parsley or garlic are commonly added for extra flavor.
The product is popular in office cafeterias and as a quick snack.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Poultry meat supplies essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The light dressing reduces saturated fat intake, making the salad suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey are rich in B3 (niacin) and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The salad provides potassium, phosphorus and iron, important for cardiovascular and blood health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables add fiber that helps maintain regular digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Light dressings often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium should watch portion size.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the salad refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain versions may contain preservatives such as sorbate, which can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the package. For extra freshness you can add more raw vegetables, herbs, or a squeeze of lemon. It pairs well with whole‑grain bread or a wrap.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. Do not freeze. After opening, consume within 2‑3 days and discard if it develops an off odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy, peanut butter filled are small sweets coated with milk or dark chocolate and filled with a smooth peanut butter paste. They are popular as a quick snack and are commonly found in confectionery assortments.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first peanut‑butter‑filled candy recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
Peanut butter filling is usually made from roasted peanuts, sugar, and a small amount of vegetable oil.
Chocolate shells can contain up to 30 % cocoa butter, giving them a glossy snap.
These candies are often used in marketing as an “energy‑boosting” snack because of the sugar‑protein combo.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides plant‑based protein that helps support muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Peanuts are rich in monounsaturated fats that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peanuts contain niacin, thiamine, and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate supplies flavonoids that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Quick energy snack
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from chocolate and fats with protein from peanuts provides a rapid energy boost.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: These candies can trigger severe allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to peanuts.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The added sugar makes them calorie‑dense and may contribute to tooth decay if consumed frequently.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A typical serving (≈30 g) can contain 150–180 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Some manufacturers use partially hydrogenated oils in the chocolate coating; choose trans‑fat‑free versions when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the candies straight from the package, stir them into ice cream or yogurt, or use them as a sweet filling in baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to prevent the chocolate shell from melting.

content.title: About
content.content: The Butterscotch Brownie Cookie is a soft, aromatic cookie featuring a rich buttery toffee flavor and chunks of chocolate brownie. The dough is made from wheat flour, butter, sugar, and eggs, then folded with butterscotch caramel pieces and bite‑size brownie bits that create a moist, flavorful center.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The butterscotch‑brownie combination was first introduced in 2015 by a craft bakery in San Francisco.
The cookie has a slightly crisp edge and a chewy, almost cake‑like interior.
Natural butterscotch syrup, free of artificial flavors, is used to achieve the signature caramel taste.
Each batch is lightly dusted with sea salt to accentuate the sweetness of the caramel.
The cookie is often paired with hot coffee or a milkshake for a balanced treat.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat provide quick energy for the body.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The chocolate brownie component supplies iron, which supports blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour contribute B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that aid metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa in the brownie offers flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Moderate sodium
items.content: A light sea‑salt topping enhances flavor without excessive sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookie contains wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Butterscotch syrup and brownie pieces make the cookie sweet; those monitoring blood sugar should limit portions.

items.title: Nut and dairy allergies
items.content: Recipes may include nuts or dairy; check the ingredient list if you have related allergies.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of sugar and fat, the cookie is relatively calorie‑dense, so moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the Butterscotch Brownie Cookie as a snack on its own, with tea or coffee, or crumble it over ice cream, yogurt, or desserts for added texture and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container at room temperature in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life (over two weeks), keep them refrigerated to maintain a soft center.

hot-dog-sandwich-nfs-on-wheat-bun.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, NFS, on Wheat Bun

content.title: About
content.content: A hot‑dog sandwich is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a grilled or boiled sausage placed inside a soft wheat bun. The NFS (No‑Frills Style) version features minimal toppings: just the sausage, bun, and a basic sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hot dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became popular with railroad travelers.
Wheat buns for hot dogs usually contain a small amount of sugar and oil, giving them a soft, slightly sweet texture.
The NFS variant is often served without extra toppings to highlight the flavor of the sausage itself.
American sausages are typically made from a blend of beef, pork, and sometimes turkey, seasoned with paprika, garlic, and other spices.
The hot dog is an iconic symbol of American culture and frequently appears in movies and advertising.

items.title: Quick Energy Source
items.content: The sausage provides protein and fat for rapid energy, while the wheat bun supplies carbohydrates.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Sausage is a source of animal protein, essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: B‑Vitamins
items.content: Sausages contain B1, B2, and B12 vitamins that support metabolic processes.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Meat products, including sausages, contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High Sodium Content
items.content: Sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated Fats
items.content: A significant portion of the fat in sausages is saturated, which may increase cholesterol levels.

items.title: Preservatives and Nitrites
items.content: Nitrites are commonly used to preserve color and shelf life, and excessive intake may be harmful.

items.title: Gluten Allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: Hot dogs are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot dogs are typically eaten warm, gently pressing the bun around the sausage. Optional condiments include mustard, ketchup, mayonnaise, or pickles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sausages in the refrigerator at +2…+4 °C and keep buns in a dry place in a sealed bag. For longer storage, sausages can be frozen, and buns can be kept in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned pineapple (NFS) consists of bite‑size pieces of ripe pineapple that have been hot‑sterilized and sealed in glass or metal jars with their own syrup. The product retains the sweet‑tart flavor and characteristic tropical aroma of fresh pineapple.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down proteins.
Canning allows pineapple to be stored for 2‑3 years without loss of taste or nutrients.
In the United States pineapple is a symbol of hospitality and is often served in cocktails and desserts.
The syrup left after canning is rich in vitamin C and B1 and can be used in cooking.
Pineapple was first introduced to Europe in the 16th century by Portuguese explorers.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis, promoting healthy skin.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain improves digestion, reduces inflammation, and may help muscle recovery after exercise.

items.title: Source of manganese
items.content: Manganese is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and fatty‑acid synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned pineapple contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports normal bowel function and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The syrup may contain added sugar, which is important for people managing diabetes.

items.title: Bromelain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bromelain, such as swelling or itching.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may include preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate); those with sensitivities should choose preservative‑free options.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of pineapple can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned pineapple can be enjoyed as a snack, added to fruit salads, yogurts, smoothies, baked goods, or used in sauces for meat and seafood. Before use, shake the jar well and drain excess syrup if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the pineapple in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Fat‑free spaghetti sauce is a ready‑to‑use tomato sauce made without added plant or animal fats. It contains ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic, herbs and spices, and a small amount of sugar to balance flavor. The product is suitable for low‑fat diets and can serve as a quick base for pasta dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce contains virtually 0 g of fat while preserving the classic Italian flavor.
Tomatoes used in the recipe are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
The product is gluten‑free and suitable for most people with food sensitivities.
Only natural herbs such as basil and oregano are used, with no artificial flavorings.
It can be heated in a microwave or on the stove in 2–3 minutes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of fat makes the sauce appropriate for calorie‑restricted diets and weight management.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene present in tomatoes has antioxidant properties and may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes provide a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Tomatoes and spices stimulate gastric juice production, improving digestion.

items.title: Moderate sodium
items.content: The sauce contains a modest amount of salt, beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tomatoes or other ingredients in the sauce.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although small, the sugar should be considered by people monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes are naturally acidic, which can cause discomfort for those with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the sauce in a saucepan or microwave, pour over cooked spaghetti and stir. It can be enhanced with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or vegetables. The sauce also works as a base for casseroles, lasagna, and seafood dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in its sealed container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, use within 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 3 months in an airtight container.

wonton-dumpling-or-pot-sticker-steamed.title: Wonton, dumpling or pot sticker, steamed

content.title: About
content.content: Wonton is a traditional Asian dish consisting of a thin wheat flour wrapper filled with meat, seafood, vegetables, or a combination thereof. Wontons can be steamed, boiled, or fried; steamed wontons have a delicate texture and retain the flavor of the filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wontons originate from Chinese cuisine, where they are known as jiaozi or baozi depending on the region.
The thin wrapper is usually made from wheat flour and water without eggs, giving it a smooth elasticity.
In different countries, wontons are served with various dipping sauces such as soy sauce, vinegar, chili oil, or aromatic broth.
Steamed wontons are often added to soups, where they absorb the broth’s flavor.
In Japan, a similar item is the gyoza, which is frequently pan‑fried to a crispy finish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat, fish, or tofu fillings provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat when steamed
items.content: Steaming requires no added oil, keeping the dish low in saturated fat.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and fish fillings supply B12, while vegetable fillings add B6 and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Wontons can provide iron, zinc, and selenium from animal or seafood ingredients, important for immune function.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The thin wrapper and gentle steam cooking make wontons soft and easy on the digestive system, suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Fillings may contain shellfish, soy sauce, or gluten, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: If not cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C, there is a risk of bacterial contamination.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Accompanying sauces are often salty; people with hypertension should limit their use.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The wheat‑based wrapper contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve wontons hot, often in broth or with soy sauce, vinegar, and chili. They can be added to soups, salads, or enjoyed as a standalone snack. Allow a brief cool‑down before eating to prevent the wrapper from tearing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh dough should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours, while cooked wontons can be stored in an airtight container at 0‑4 °C for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze the wontons on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag – they keep quality for up to 2 months. Thaw frozen wontons in the refrigerator before cooking.
